tagline.text: A joint showcase of Cordillera festivals, held in Baguio each October

location.label: Location
location.text: Around Session Road, Baguio City (host city changes, confirm each year)

best_season.label: Best time to visit
best_season.text: October (Indigenous Peoples' Month), confirm the date

budget.label: Budget
budget.text: About ₱3,000~9,000 (1–2 nights in Baguio, including round-trip bus from Manila)

children.text: Representative festivals from the six provinces and two cities of the Cordillera perform together at this regional event. The Department of Tourism's Cordillera office started it in 2022, and it is held as a street parade on Session Road in Baguio each October.

The Cordillera Festival of Festivals, as the name says, brings together the many festivals of the Cordillera Administrative Region (CAR) in one place. It is run by the Department of Tourism's Cordillera office (DOT-CAR) and began in October 2022 in Baguio as a pilot to test whether in-person festivals could draw tourists again after COVID-19. It was held in Baguio every year after that, and several news outlets report that Kalinga is due to host for the first time in 2027. The dates and venue have not been announced yet, so confirm them through official announcements.

The participants are the six provinces of Abra, Apayao, Benguet, Ifugao, Kalinga and Mountain Province, plus the two cities of Baguio and Tabuk. Each team performs a short version of its area's signature festival in dance and ritual, so the big attraction is seeing the culture of the Cordillera in a single day without traveling around. In 2026 more than 500 performers were announced. The original festivals each have their own main stage elsewhere. Kalinga's Bodong Festival takes place in February and honors the bodong peace pact system (the 2023 edition reportedly set two Guinness records, with 3,440 gong players and 4,681 banga dancers). Apayao's Say-am began in 1996 and is held around its February 14 founding anniversary, Mountain Province's Lang-ay runs for a week in April in Bontoc, and Benguet's Adivay is held in November. Abra's Kawayan honors bamboo, and Baguio's Panagbenga is a modern festival that began in 1996 and lasts all of February. This event offers only a taste of the key scenes from these festivals.

The event is usually held in October because October is Indigenous Peoples' Month in the Philippines. In 2024 it was on October 18; in 2025 the street parade was held on October 24 as part of events on October 22–26; and in 2026 it was on October 17. If you plan to see it, allow for the fact that the date and route change every year.
This page covers this one event only. For the city as a whole and general sightseeing such as Session Road and Burnham Park, see

blocks.title: Eight Cordillera festivals in one line

children.text: Abra's Kawayan, Benguet's Adivay, Ifugao's Gotad, Kalinga's Bodong, Apayao's Say-am, Mountain Province's Lang-ay, Tabuk's Matagoan and Baguio's Panagbenga pass by in turn. Each team comes out in the costumes and instruments of its home area. In 2024 Ifugao presented Kulpi ad Ifugao, a ritual asking for protection of the crop after rice planting, and in 2025 and 2026 it brought Gotad ad Ifugao.

blocks.title: A street parade that stops to dance

children.text: Teams start from the upper end of Session Road and move down, stopping at set points to dance. In 2024 they gathered after sunrise and marched to Malcolm Square. It is a close-up event that you can follow on foot.

Meaningful dances follow one another: a harvest dance from Mountain Province, a wedding dance from Ifugao, Benguet's victory dance bendian, and Kalinga's gabbok, a ritual dedicating a first-born child. The sound of gongs adds to the sense of being there.

blocks.title: A closing dance that unites everyone

children.text: Near the end all the performers join in a "Unifying Dance." In 2025 the Secretary of Tourism was reported to have joined the final dance.

In 2025 awards were announced, including Best Traditional Performance (Adivay of Benguet), Most Creative Choreography (Kawayan of Abra) and Crowd Favorite (Panagbenga of Baguio). A market exhibit of crafts, local products and traditional garments was also held at Malcolm Square.

blocks.title: Together with Indigenous Peoples' Month events

children.text: Because it falls in October's Indigenous Peoples' Month, the event comes with programs introducing local artisans, culture-bearers and producers. You can find crafts that are hard to get at other times.
The street parade can be watched free from the roadside. October is a rainy time, but with a raincoat you can enjoy it fully in a single day.

items.title: Parade day, 2 days 1 night
items.subtitle: Arrive the day before, watch the parade and stroll through town

children.text: Arrive in Baguio by night or daytime bus from Manila and check in at a lodging near Session Road. Rooms fill quickly in event week.
Have dinner at the Harrison Road night market or a restaurant in town and turn in early. The parade often starts in the morning.
Go to the upper end of Session Road and confirm the announced start time. In 2024 the teams gathered after sunrise.
Watch the team performances as you walk down Session Road. Follow the procession and watch at the points where each team stops.
Watch the exhibit market and the closing dance at Malcolm Square.
Have lunch at a Session Road restaurant and stroll through Burnham Park.
Visit Baguio Cathedral or Mines View Park, then take a bus back to Manila.
Start times, routes and venues change every year. Check the official notice from the Department of Tourism's Cordillera office.
Victory Liner, JoyBus and Solid North buses run almost around the clock from Cubao, Pasay, PITX and other terminals in Manila. Via TPLEX the trip takes about
4–6 hours

Tickets sell out fast on holidays and during event week. Book in advance on the official app or online.
Public transport fares may be revised, so check the latest fare when you book.
A direct bus from Clark International Airport (CRK) to the Governor Pack Road terminal in Baguio takes about
3–4 hours

There are only about five departures a day, so match them to your flight's arrival time.
Take NLEX–SCTEX–TPLEX, exit at Rosales or Pozorrubio and climb on Marcos Highway. It takes about
4–5 hours
Kennon Road is often closed because of rockfalls and repairs, so check beforehand whether it is passable.
The Session Road and Burnham Park area can be covered on foot, and a jeepney ride costs about
Most taxis are white; ask the driver to turn on the meter. Roads around Session Road are closed on parade day, so move early and on foot.

Because the event is held around October, it overlaps with Baguio's rainy season. In 2025 showers passed on parade day, but the event went ahead as planned. Bring a raincoat and keep one indoor activity ready in case of rain.
Baguio is cool all year, but mornings are colder. Bring a light jacket. In the rainy season typhoons can block mountain roads, so check the forecast before you travel.

For reference, Baguio is one of the wettest cities in the Philippines, with annual rainfall of about 3,800mm concentrated in the June–October rainy season. Fog and rain are common even in mid-October, so plan to watch the parade ready to get wet.

items.label: Lodging (guesthouse)
items.note: Per night, may rise in event week

children.text: Prices are approximate as of
and may vary with local conditions.
The most convenient lodging is near Session Road and Burnham Park. You can walk to the market, night market and restaurants, and the bus terminals are close. Guesthouses cost about
a night and mid-range hotels about

, and prices can nearly double during Panagbenga and Holy Week. Event week is similarly busy, so book early. Many places in Baguio have no air conditioning, but hot water and thick blankets are standard.

As befits a highland city, food centers on fresh vegetables, strawberries and coffee. Benguet vegetable salads and soups, etag (Cordillera-style smoked pork) and, on cold nights, bulalo, a hot beef-shank soup, all go well. The cheap rice eateries on the second floor of the public market are good when you want to eat like a local. On parade day roadside restaurants can be crowded, so have lunch a little early.
The date, start time and route change every year. Before you go, check the social media of the Department of Tourism's Cordillera office and notices from Baguio city.
In 2024 teams gathered at the upper end of Session Road and finished at Malcolm Square, while in 2025 they started from the Melvin Jones Football Field. Confirm the start and end points first.
Mornings are cold, so bring a jacket. Short sleeves may be enough in the daytime, but it turns chilly when it rains.
Roads are closed, so walking is faster than taking a taxi. Much of the city is uphill, so comfortable walking shoes are a must.
Keep your camera and phone under your raincoat and carry your bag in front. Watch for pickpockets in crowds.
It is polite to ask performers before photographing them. Avoid filming during traditional rituals.
This is a one-day event, so combine it with sightseeing in Baguio or a mountain trip such as Sagada the next day.
To see an individual festival properly, check when its main stage takes place. Kalinga's Bodong is said to be in February, Mountain Province's Lang-ay in April and Benguet's Adivay in November.
October is a season of typhoons and rain. Mountain roads may be blocked or landslides may occur before and after the event, so check the PAGASA forecast and road conditions before you travel.
The event schedule and route change every year and may be altered. Official announcements are the most accurate.
Roads around Session Road are closed and traffic is heavy on event day. Do not bring a car.
Baguio is at about 1,500m, so you may feel slightly short of breath. Take it easy on the first day.
Beware of pickpockets at the night market and public market, and take another taxi if the driver demands a flat fare.
Baguio has strict ordinances on smoking, single-use plastic and noise. Follow local rules.
